941.event_title: Christiaan Eijkman traces beriberi to polished rice
941.place: Batavia, Java, Dutch East Indies (now Jakarta, Indonesia)
941.event: Working in the Dutch government's medical laboratory in Batavia, Christiaan Eijkman found that chickens fed on polished white rice developed a nerve disease resembling beriberi and recovered when they were given unpolished rice. He at first explained this as a harmful substance in the rice grain that the outer layer counteracted, but the finding was later understood as the lack of a vital substance in the rice's outer layer. The work led to the concept of vitamins and earned Eijkman the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
941.explanation: Eijkman's experiment helped show that illness can come not only from something harmful being present but from something necessary being missing, a turning point in medical thinking.
941.tie_back: The kural says the body's forces cause disease whether they grow too strong or fall too low, and Eijkman's beriberi work moved from a theory of harmful excess to the discovery that a deficiency was to blame.
941._accuracy_note: Next-best: the event illustrates the excess-or-deficiency idea of disease, but it concerns a vitamin, not the three humours of Ayurvedic and Siddha theory.

942.event_title: William Beaumont observes digestion through Alexis St. Martin's stomach
942.place: Fort Mackinac, Michigan Territory, and other army posts, United States
942.event: In 1822 army surgeon William Beaumont treated Alexis St. Martin, a young French-Canadian trapper accidentally wounded by a gunshot, whose wound healed leaving a permanent opening into his stomach. From 1825 Beaumont used the opening to observe digestion directly, timing how long different foods took to be digested and having gastric juice analysed, which showed it contained hydrochloric acid. He published his results in 1833 as Experiments and Observations on the Gastric Juice and the Physiology of Digestion; modern historians also note that his treatment of St. Martin raises serious ethical questions.
942.explanation: Beaumont's work established that digestion is a chemical process that takes measurable time, giving scientific shape to the old advice not to eat before the last meal has been dealt with.
942.tie_back: The kural makes complete digestion of the previous meal the test for eating again, and Beaumont was the first to watch and time that process inside a living human stomach.
942._accuracy_note: Next-best: the event shows that digestion takes time and can be observed, but it does not demonstrate the kural's claim that waiting for digestion makes medicine unnecessary.

943.event_title: Alvise Cornaro writes his Treatise on the Sober Life
943.event: Alvise (Luigi) Cornaro, a businessman and patron of the arts in Padua, became critically ill around the age of forty after years of intemperate living and resolved to follow strict rules on the quantity and quality of what he ate and drank. He recovered, and in 1558 published his Treatise on the Sober Life, describing his measured diet as the source of his health and recommending moderation as the way to live to a great age. He revised and added to the work in the following years, lived into his eighties, and died in 1566; the book became an international success and was translated into English many times.
943.explanation: Cornaro's book is one of the earliest and most widely read personal accounts of measured eating as a path to long life.
943.tie_back: The kural says that one who eats in the right measure after digestion keeps the body going for a long time, which is exactly the regimen and result Cornaro described.
943._accuracy_note: Very close fit to measured eating and longevity; his exact birth year is uncertain, so his age at death is stated only generally.

944.event_title: Willem Dicke shows that wheat harms children with coeliac disease
944.event: Dutch paediatrician Willem Karel Dicke presented a doctoral thesis at the University of Utrecht in 1950 showing that wheat flour and rye flour caused the symptoms of coeliac disease in children, while purified wheat starch did not. He had suspected wheat since the 1930s, and observations during the wartime Dutch famine of 1944-45, when bread was scarce, reinforced his view. His work, followed by the identification of gluten as the harmful part of the grain, made the gluten-free diet the standard treatment.
944.explanation: Dicke showed that a food that nourishes most people can be harmful to some, so that health depends on choosing foods that suit one's own body.
944.tie_back: The kural tells us to keep firmly to foods that agree with the body, and Dicke's patients recovered once a food that disagreed with their constitution was removed.
944._accuracy_note: Strong fit to the kural's idea of foods that do or do not agree with the body; the kural's second point, eating only when truly hungry, is not illustrated.

945.event_title: Finland launches the North Karelia Project
945.event: In the early 1970s the Finnish province of North Karelia had one of the highest rates of death from heart disease in the world, and in 1972 local authorities, working with the World Health Organization, launched a community-wide programme to change how people lived. It encouraged residents to replace butter and whole milk with lower-fat alternatives, eat more vegetables and less salt, and stop smoking, and worked with schools and local food producers to change what was on offer. Over the following decades heart-disease deaths among working-age people in the region fell by roughly 80 percent, though the exact figure varies with the period measured.
945.explanation: The project became a world model for preventing illness by changing everyday diet across a whole community rather than treating disease after it appears.
945.tie_back: The kural promises that no harm comes to the life of one who eats wholesome food and holds back from excess, and North Karelia showed that promise borne out across a whole population.
945._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit to wholesome eating and avoiding harmful excess, but the project also targeted smoking and blood pressure, so diet was not the only cause of the improvement.

946.event: Kaibara Ekiken, a scholar of the Fukuoka Domain who had also studied medicine, wrote the Yojokun (Lessons on Nourishing Life) at the age of 83, and it was published in 1713. The handbook advised balanced, moderate eating and stopping at about eight-tenths full, alongside exercise, sound sleep and a calm mind. Written in plain Japanese rather than classical Chinese, it became one of the most widely read health books in Japan and is still reprinted today; Kaibara himself lived to 86.
946.explanation: The Yojokun spread the principle of stopping before one is full, still known in Japan as hara hachi bu, to generations of ordinary readers.
946.tie_back: The kural says well-being stays with one who knows to eat a little less, which is the very rule of eating to eight-tenths that Kaibara taught.
946._accuracy_note: Strong fit to the first half of the kural (eating a little less brings well-being); the second half, disease clinging to the glutton, is implied rather than shown.

947.event_title: King Henry I of England dies after a meal of lampreys
947.event: Henry I, king of England and duke of Normandy, fell ill and died at Lyons-la-Forêt in Normandy on 1 December 1135. The chronicler Henry of Huntingdon recorded that the king's last illness followed a meal of lampreys, a fish he was fond of, eaten against medical advice. His death without a surviving legitimate son led to a long succession war between his nephew Stephen and his daughter Matilda.
947.explanation: The account of the king's last meal became a byword in English history for the danger of indulging an appetite against good advice.
947.tie_back: The kural warns that one who thoughtlessly eats beyond what the body can digest will suffer disease beyond measure, and the chroniclers presented Henry's fatal illness in just those terms.
947._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit; the meal is recorded by a twelfth-century chronicler and repeated by historians, but the exact medical cause of death cannot be confirmed.

948.event_title: Walter Reed's commission confirms that mosquitoes spread yellow fever
948.event: In 1900 the United States Army sent a commission led by Walter Reed to Cuba to study yellow fever, which was killing soldiers and civilians. Testing the hypothesis of the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay, the commission showed that the disease was carried by a mosquito and not spread by contact with patients' clothing or bedding. William Gorgas then directed a campaign in Havana to screen patients and destroy mosquito breeding places, and within months of its start in 1901 the city was freed of yellow fever.
948.explanation: Identifying the true cause of the disease made an effective remedy possible, and the same methods later protected workers building the Panama Canal.
948.tie_back: The kural's method is to find the disease, find its cause, find what will relieve it and then act, and the Reed commission and Gorgas followed that sequence step by step.
948._accuracy_note: Close to a dramatisation of the kural's diagnosis-cause-remedy-action sequence.

949.event_title: Dominique-Jean Larrey introduces flying ambulances and triage
949.place: French Revolutionary and Napoleonic armies, Europe
949.event: Dominique-Jean Larrey, a surgeon in the French army, introduced horse-drawn flying ambulances in the 1790s to carry wounded soldiers from the battlefield quickly instead of leaving them until the fighting ended. He also insisted that the wounded be treated in order of how badly they were hurt and how urgently they needed care, not according to their rank. His system of sorting casualties is regarded as the origin of modern triage.
949.explanation: Larrey made the patient's condition and the urgency of the moment, rather than social standing, the basis for medical decisions.
949.tie_back: The kural asks the physician to weigh the patient, the extent of the disease and the time before acting, and Larrey's triage did exactly that on the battlefield.
949._accuracy_note: Strong fit to weighing the patient, the disease and timing; the kural's sense of season and climate is not covered.

950.event_title: Albert Alexander becomes the first patient treated with penicillin
950.event: Albert Alexander, a police constable with a severe infection, became the first patient to receive penicillin made by Howard Florey's team at Oxford, and within a day his fever fell and the infection began to heal. The drug was so scarce that the team recovered it from his urine to use again, but after five days the supply ran out; he relapsed and died on 15 March 1941. Norman Heatley, who had turned the laboratory into a small penicillin factory, later travelled with Florey to the United States to help start large-scale production.
950.explanation: The case showed that a cure needs not only a sick person, a skilled doctor and a good remedy, but also someone able to prepare enough of that remedy.
950.tie_back: The kural names four parts of medicine, patient, physician, remedy and the one who prepares it, and Alexander's case showed that when the fourth part could not keep up, even a true cure failed.
950._accuracy_note: Very close fit: all four parts of the kural appear, and the failure of supply shows why each one is needed.
